---
title: "Experimental design"
---

A statistical model begins after observations have been collected. By that point, however, many of the decisions that determine what the observations can tell us have already been made. Someone has chosen which speakers, sentences, recordings, or languages may enter the study. Someone has also decided which unit receives each condition, which responses are measured, and which observations will be retained. Recall from [turning linguistic records into data](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd) that the unit represented by a row need not be the unit to which a claim applies. The model cannot undo those decisions.

The design determines whether the observed comparison can identify the [estimand introduced in the foundations module](../foundations/making-sense-of-data.qmd). If the estimand is a mean difference between two training procedures, for instance, then the design must produce comparable groups that differ systematically in training procedure. A precise model fitted to groups that differed before training does not repair a design that fails to identify the intended mean difference.

::: {.callout-note title="Reading: Winter (2020), Sections 14.2 and 14.3"}
[Winter, *The independence assumption* and *Dealing with non-independence via experimental design and averaging*, in *Statistics for Linguists*](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf).

**Why this reading?** These sections begin with the repeated observations common in linguistic research and ask which observations may count as independent evidence. They are included here because the same question governs assignment, counterbalancing, exclusion, and design simulation throughout this module.
:::

## A design is a sequence of commitments

Consider an experiment on the recognition of words in two accents. A useful design description answers seven questions in order.

1. What unit can independently receive an accent condition?
2. What procedure assigns conditions to those units?
3. Does each participant encounter one condition or more than one condition?
4. Which item versions does each participant encounter?
5. Which observations will enter the analysis?
6. What numerical comparison estimates the intended accent contrast?
7. Under a plausible data-generating process, how often will the planned procedure support the stated decision?

Each answer constrains the answers that follow. If accent is assigned once per participant, trials from that participant are not separate assignments. If every participant encounters both accents, the comparison is made within participants and order may matter. If failures to respond are removed more often in one accent, the retained comparison may target only trials on which a response was produced. The seven questions are thus parts of one design, even though we introduce them separately.

## Repeated rows are not repeated designs

Linguistic datasets often contain more than one repeated unit. Participants respond to several items, and items are presented to several participants. A table with 2,000 rows may have only 40 independently assigned participants, 50 sentence items, or some combination determined by the design. The row count says how many responses were recorded. It does not, by itself, say how many independent opportunities the study had to compare conditions.

Software places every response in a row, but a row does not show how its condition was assigned. The first page separates the [unit of assignment](units-of-assignment.qmd) from the unit of observation and the [unit of analysis introduced earlier](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd). [Random assignment](random-assignment.qmd) then describes how conditions reach the units of assignment.

## Chapter sequence

After assignment, we distinguish [within-participant designs](within-participant-designs.qmd), in which a participant contributes to more than one condition, from [between-participant designs](between-participant-designs.qmd), in which a participant contributes to only one. [Counterbalancing](counterbalancing.qmd) then distributes item versions across lists while preserving the intended contrast. [Exclusion rules](exclusion-rules.qmd) define the analyzed set, and [power by simulation](power-by-simulation.qmd) evaluates the complete planned procedure under stated assumptions.

The pages introduce one design object at a time. They do not yet introduce models for grouped data. Instead, each page records the participants, items, blocks, or sites whose shared variation a later analysis must preserve. This ordering keeps the statistical method subordinate to the linguistic comparison.

## Learning outcomes

By the end of the module, we should be able to reconstruct how a condition reached each observation, state which comparisons were made possible by that procedure, and identify where exclusions or imbalance may have changed the target. These capabilities prepare us to represent repeated participants and items without pretending that a model can create experimental replication after collection.
